¶
'''awk<sup>1</sup>†''' (âk), ''adv.'' [< ''awk''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.''] Awkwardly; wrongly.
{{smaller block|Professors ringing as ''awk'' as the bells.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange'', Fables, ccci.}}}}

'''awk<sup>2</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''auk''<sup>1</sup>.

'''awkerd, awkert''' (â′kėrd, -kėrt), ''a.'' A dialectal form of ''awkward''. [Prov. Eng.]

'''awkly†''' (âk′li), ''adv.'' [ME. ''awkely''; < ''awk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.] In the wrong direction; left- or back-handedly. Hence—(''a'') Awkwardly; clumsily. (''b'') Perversely. (''c'') Untowardly; unluckily.

'''awkly†''' (âk′li), ''a.'' [< ''awk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. AS. (ONorth.) ''afulīc'', perverse: see ''awk''<sup>1</sup>.] Perverse; untoward.

'''awkness†''' (âk′nes), ''n.'' [< ''awk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness''.] The state of being awk or awkward.

'''awkward''' (âk′wärd), ''adv.'' [Early mod. E. or dial. also ''aukward, awkwart, awkard, awkerd, awkert'', etc., ME. ''awkwarde, aukward'', etc., transversely, sidewise, perversely; < ''awk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ward''.] '''1†.''' In the wrong direction; in the wrong way; backward.
{{smaller block|<poem>The emperour thane egerly at Arthure he strykez,
''Awkwarde'' on the umbrere [vizor] and egerly hym hittez.</poem>
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2247.}}}}
'''2†.''' Asquint.—'''3.''' Awkwardly; clumsily. [Now only prov. Eng.]

'''awkward''' (âk′wärd), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. or dial. also ''aukward, awkwart, awkard, awkerd'', etc.; < ''awkward'', ''adv.''] '''1†.''' Turned the wrong way; backhanded.—'''2†.''' Perverted; perverse.
{{smaller block|They with ''awkward'' judgment put the chief point of godliness in outward things.
{{right|''Udall'', Mat. v.}}}}
{{smaller block|’Tis no sinister nor no ''awkward'' claim.}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|aween|400|awkwardly}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''aween†''', ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''awenen'', < ''a-'' + ''wenen'', < AS. ''wēnan'', think, ween: see ''a-''<sup>1</sup> and ''ween''.]   To ween; suppose.
{{smaller block|The Jewes out of Jurselem ''awenden'' he were wode [mad].
{{right|''Rel. Ant.'', I. 144.}}}}

'''aweigh''' (a-wā′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.''   [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''weigh''.]   ''Naut.'', atrip. {{smaller|The anchor is ''aweigh'' when it is just drawn from its hold in the ground and hangs perpendicularly. See ''atrip''.}}

'''aweless''' (â′les), ''a.''   [< ME. ''awles'', etc.; AS. ''egeleás'', < ''ege'', awe (see ''awe''<sup>1</sup>), + ''-leás'', -less.]   '''1.''' Wanting awe or reverence; void of deferential fear.
{{smaller block|<poem>Lordes bene lawles,
Chyldere bene ''awles''.</poem>
{{right|''A Prophecy'', etc., l. 16 (E. E. T. S., extra ser., VIII. i. 85).}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''aweless'' lion could not wage the fight.
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Wanting the power of inspiring reverence or awe.
{{smaller block|The innocent and ''awless'' throne.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., ii. 4.}}}}
Also spelled ''awless''.

'''awesome''' (â′sum), ''a.''   [North. E. and Sc.; < ''awe''<sup>1</sup> + ''-some''.]   '''1.''' Inspiring awe; awful: as, an ''awesome'' sight.
{{smaller block|“An ''awsome'' place,” answered the blind woman, “as ever living creature took refuge in.”
{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, xliii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Wizard, on his part, manfully stuck up for his price, declaring that to raise the Devil was really no joke, and insinuating that to do so was an ''awesome'' crime.
{{right|''Kinglake'', Eothen, p. 168.}}}}
'''2.''' Evidencing or expressive of terror.
{{smaller block|He did gie an ''awesome'' glance up at the auld castle.
{{right|''Scott'', Guy Mannering, I. xi.}}}} Also spelled ''awsome.''

'''awe-strike''' (â′strīk), ''v. t.'' To strike with awe. [Rare.]

'''awe-struck''' (â′struk), ''p. a.'' Impressed or struck with awe.

'''awful''' (â′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''awful, agheful, aghful;'' AS. ''egeful,'' < ''ege,'' awe (see ''awe''<sup>1</sup>), + ''-ful.'']   '''1.''' Striking or inspiring with awe; filling with dread, or dread mingled with profound reverence: as, the ''awful'' majesty of Jehovah; the ''awful'' approach of death.
{{smaller block|<poem>Her fathers’ God before her moved,
An ''awful'' guide in smoke and flame.</poem>
{{right|''Scott,'' When Israel, of the Lord beloved.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''awful'' mysteries of the world unseen. {{right|''J. Caird.''}}}}
'''2.''' Of a dreadful character; causing fear or horror; terrible; appalling: as, an ''awful'' disaster; I heard an ''awful'' shriek.
{{smaller block|<poem>Or if she slept, she dream’d
An ''awful'' dream.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson,'' Guinevere.}}}}
'''3†.''' Inspiring or commanding respect, reverence, or obedience.
{{smaller block|An ''awful'' rule and right supremacy.
{{right|''Shak.,'' T. of the S., v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A parish priest was of the pilgrim train;
An ''awful,'' reverend, and religious man.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden,'' Char. of Good Parson, l. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|She would, upon occasions, treat them with freedom; yet her demeanour was so ''awful,'' that they durst not fail in the least point of respect. {{right|''Swift,'' Death of Stella.}}}}
'''4.''' Expressive of or indicating deep awe, as for the Deity.
{{smaller block|<poem>Towards him they bend
With ''awful'' reverence prone.</poem>
{{right|''Milton,'' P. L., ii. 478.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Awful'' prostration, like Pascal’s, before the divine idea. {{right|''De Quincey'', Secret Societies, i.}}}}

'''5†.''' Impressed with or exhibiting respect or reverence, as for authority; law-abiding; respectful in the extreme.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thrust from the company of ''awful'' men.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>How dare thy joints forget
To pay their ''awful'' duty to our presence?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., iii. 3.}}}}

'''6.''' Having some character in an extreme or noticeable degree; excessive; very great; extraordinary; preposterous: as, he is an ''awful'' dandy; that is an ''awful'' bonnet. [Colloq. and vulgar.]
{{smaller block|Pot-pie is the favorite dish, and woodsmen, sharp-set, are ''awful'' eaters.
{{right|''Carleton'', New Purchase, I. 182. (''Bartlett.'')}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1''' and '''2.''' ''Awful, Dreadful, Fearful, Frightful,'' solemn, imposing, majestic; dread, dire, dreadful, terrible. The first four of these words are often loosely or colloquially used to express dislike, detestation, or horror, but should in the main retain the same distinctions of meaning as the nouns from which they are derived. Thus, ''awful'' is full of awe, full of that which inspires awe, exciting a feeling of deep solemnity and reverence, often with a certain admixture of fear, acting especially upon the imagination (see ''reverence, n.''); the suggestion may shift in all degrees from awe to horror: as, an ''awful'' steamboat explosion. ''Dreadful'' is applied to what inspires dread, that is, an oppressive fear of coming evil, and loosely to what is very bad. ''Fearful'', full of fear, impressing fear: as, “a certain ''fearful'' looking for of judgment,” Heb. x. 27. ''Frightful'', not full of fright, but inspiring fright or sudden and almost paralyzing fear. An ''awful'' sight; a ''dreadful'' disaster; a ''fearful'' leap; a ''frightful'' chasm.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Abash’d the Devil stood,
And felt how ''awful'' goodness is.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iv. 846.}}}}
{{smaller block|The smoothness of flattery cannot save us in this rugged and ''awful'' crisis. {{right|''Chatham'', Speech on American War.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O Lord! methought what pain it was to drown!
What ''dreadful'' noise of waters in mine ears!
What sights of ugly death within mine eyes!
Methought I saw a thousand ''fearful'' wracks.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., i. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|There was a ''fearful'', sullen sound of rushing waves and broken surges. {{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 21.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Their music, ''frightful'' as the serpents’ hiss.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2.}}}}

'''awfully''' (â′fụl-i), ''adv.'' In an awful manner. {{smaller|(''a'') Dreadfully; terribly. (''b'') With solemn impressiveness; sublimely; majestically. (''c'') With a feeling of awe or reverential fear; reverently. (''d'') Excessively; extremely; very: as, an ''awfully'' jolly man; an ''awfully'' pretty girl. [Slang.]}}
{{smaller block|You’ll be ''awfully'' glad to get rid of me.
{{right|''W. Black'', Green Pastures, ii.}}}}

'''awfulness''' (â′fụl-nes), ''n.'' '''1.''' The quality of being awful, or of striking or inspiring with awe, fear, or horror; impressive solemnity or sublimity; dreadfulness; terribleness: as, the ''awfulness'' of the sacred place, or of a casualty.
{{smaller block|Contrasts which move, now our laughter at their incongruity, and now our terror at their ''awfulness''. {{right|''J. Caird.''}}}}
'''2†.''' The state of being full of or inspired with awe; reverence; awe.

{{smaller block|A help to prayer producing in us reverence and ''awfulness.''
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Holy Living.}}}}

'''awgrim†''', ''n.'' A Middle English form of ''algorism.''

'''awhape†''', ''v. t.''   [Revived by Spenser from a ME. verb found only in pp. ''awhaped'', ''awaped'', terrified, confounded; a word of uncertain origin. Cf. Goth. ''afhwapjan'', choke, suffocate.]   To confound; terrify. Also ''awape.''
{{smaller block|<poem>Not fulliche alle ''awhaped'',
Out of the temple alle esiliche he wente.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 316.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A wilde and salvage man, . . .
All overgrowne with hair, that could ''awhape''
An hardy hart.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. vii. 5.}}}}

'''awheels''' (ạ-hwēlz′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''   [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''wheels.'']   On wheels.   ''B. Jonson.''

'''awhile''' (ạ-hwīl′), ''adv.'', prop. ''adv. phr.''   [< ME. ''awhile'', ''one while;'' the adv. acc. of ''a''<sup>2</sup> + ''while.'']   For a space of time; for some time; for a short time.
{{smaller block|Counsel may stop ''awhile'' what will not stay.
{{right|''Shak.'', Lover’s Complaint, l. 159.}}}}
{{smaller block|The company were all sorry to separate so soon, . . . and stood ''a-while'' looking back on the water, upon which the moonbeams played. {{right|''Dryden'', Essay on Dram. Poesy.}}}}
{{smaller block|[''Awhile'' is properly two words, as it has to be written when an adjective is used, as ''a little while'', and as it is commonly and should be always written when preceded by ''for.'']}}

'''awide†''', ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.''   [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''wide'', after ''afar'', etc.]   Wide; widely.
{{smaller block|They opened their mouth ''awide'' [''wide'' in authorized version] upon me.
{{right|Ps. xxxiv. 21 (Douay version).}}}}

'''awing''' (a-wing′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''a.'' or ''adv.''   [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''wing.'']   On the wing.
{{smaller block|’Tis time his fortune be ''a-wing;'' high time, sir.
{{right|''Fletcher'', Humorous Lieutenant, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|Moving specks, which he thought might be ships in flight or pursuit, or they might be white birds ''awing.''
{{right|''L. Wallace'', Ben-Hur, p. 161.}}}}

'''awk'''<sup>1</sup> (âk), ''a.''   [< ME. ''awke'', ''auke'', < ONorth. *''afuh'' (in ''afulic'', perverse) (= Icel. ''öfugr'', ''öfigr'' (for *''afugr'') = Sw. ''afvig'' = OS. ''abhuh'', ''abhoh'' = OHG. ''abuh'', ''abah'', ''abeh'', MHG. ''ebich'', ''ebech'', G. dial. ''abicht'', ''abech'', ''abäch'', ''äbich'', ''äbig'' = MD. ''avesch'', ''aefsch'', awkward, contrary, perverse, D. ''aafsch'', crafty, artful), lit. ‘offward,’ < ''af'', AS. ''of'', E. ''off'', away, with a suffix of variable form and obscure origin. Cf. Goth. ''ibuks'', back, backward, in which ''ib-'', like the prefix in ''ibdalja'', descent, declivity, is perhaps a var. of *''ab'', ''af'', thus making ''ibuks'' = OS. ''abhuh'', etc., = E. ''awk''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1†.''' Turned in the opposite direction; directed the wrong way; backhanded: as, “an ''awk'' stroke,” ''Palsgrave.''—'''2†.''' Left; left-handed.
{{smaller block|On the ''awk'' or left hand.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Plutarch, p. 717.}}}}
'''3†.''' Wrong; erroneous; perverse: as, the ''awk'' end of a rod.
{{smaller block|Confuting . . . the ''awk'' opinions of the Stoics.
{{right|''Golding'', tr. of De Mornay’s Trueness of Christ. Religion.}}}}
'''4.''' Awkward to use; clumsy: as, an ''awk'' tool. [Prov. Eng.]—'''5†.''' Strange; singular; distinguished.
{{smaller block|<poem>Off elders of alde tyme and of theire ''awke'' dedys,
How they were lele in theire lawe, and lovede God Almyghty.</poem>
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (ed. Perry, E. E. T. S.), l. 13.}}}}

'''awk<sup>1</sup>†''' (âk), ''adv.''   [< ''awk''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'']   Awkwardly; wrongly.
{{smaller block|Professors ringing as ''awk'' as the bells.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange'', Fables, ccci.}}}}

'''awk<sup>2</sup>''', ''n.'' See ''auk''<sup>1</sup>.

'''awkerd, awkert''' (â′kėrd, -kėrt), ''a.'' A dialectal form of ''awkward''. [Prov. Eng.]

'''awkly†''' (âk′li), ''adv.''   [ME. ''awkely''; < ''awk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>2</sup>.]   In the wrong direction; left- or back-handedly. Hence—(''a'') Awkwardly; clumsily. (''b'') Perversely. (''c'') Untowardly; unluckily.

'''awkly†''' (âk′li), ''a.''   [< ''awk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. AS. (ONorth.) ''afulīc'', perverse: see ''awk''<sup>1</sup>.]   Perverse; untoward.

'''awkness†''' (âk′nes), ''n.''   [< ''awk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness''.]   The state of being awk or awkward.

'''awkward''' (âk′wärd), ''adv.''   [Early mod. E. or dial. also ''aukward, awkwart, awkard, awkerd, awkert'', etc., ME. ''awkwarde, aukward'', etc., transversely, sidewise, perversely; < ''awk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ward''.]   '''1†.''' In the wrong direction; in the wrong way; backward.
{{smaller block|<poem>The emperour thane egerly at Arthure he strykez,
''Awkwarde'' on the umbrere [vizor] and egerly hym hittez.</poem>
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2247.}}}}
'''2†.''' Asquint.—'''3.''' Awkwardly; clumsily. [Now only prov. Eng.]

'''awkward''' (âk′wärd), ''a.''   [Early mod. E. or dial. also ''aukward, awkwart, awkard, awkerd'', etc.; < ''awkward'', ''adv.'']   '''1†.''' Turned the wrong way; backhanded.—'''2†.''' Perverted; perverse.
{{smaller block|They with ''awkward'' judgment put the chief point of godliness in outward things.
{{right|''Udall'', Mat. v.}}}}
{{smaller block|’Tis no sinister nor no ''awkward'' claim. {{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., ii. 4.}}}}
'''3†.''' Untoward; adverse.
{{smaller block|<poem>Twice by ''awkward'' wind from England’s bank
Drove back again unto my native clime.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 2.}}}}
'''4.''' Ill adapted for use or handling; unhandy in operation; clumsy: as, ''awkward'' instruments or contrivances.—'''5.''' Wanting dexterity or skill in action or movement; clumsy in doing anything, as in using tools or implements; bungling.
{{smaller block|So true that he was ''awkward'' at a trick. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''6.''' Ungraceful in action or person; ungainly; uncouth: as, ''awkward'' gestures; the ''awkward'' gambols of the elephant.
{{smaller block|<poem>Drop’d an ''awkward'' court’sy to the Knight.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Wife of Bath’s Tale.}}}}
'''7.''' Embarrassed; not at ease: used in relation to persons: as, an ''awkward'' feeling.—'''8.''' Not easily dealt with; troublesome; vexatious; requiring caution: as, an ''awkward'' predicament. [Colloq.]
{{smaller block|Between the weir and the trees it is an ''awkward'' spot, but difficulty is the charm of fly-fishing.
{{right|''Froude'', Sketches, p. 241.}}}}
'''9†.''' Unlucky.
{{smaller block|<poem>The beast long struggled as being like to prove
An ''awkward'' sacrifice.</poem>
{{right|''Marlowe.''}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 5''' and '''6.''' ''Awkward, Clumsy, Ungainly, Uncouth, Bungling,'' unhandy, inexpert, unskilful, inapt, lubberly; uncourtly, inelegant, constrained, clownish. ''Awkward'' is generally applied to want of ease and grace or skill in bodily movement, especially of the arms or legs: as, an ''awkward'' gait; ''awkward'' in the use of a tool. ''Clumsy'' starts from the notion of heaviness, and consequent unwieldiness or awkwardness in use; it is applicable to the whole body or to any part of it, even when still: as, a ''clumsy'' figure; ''clumsy'' hands. This difference is also found in the figurative use of the words: a ''clumsy'' excuse is one that is put together badly; an ''awkward'' excuse is one that may be good, but is not gracefully presented. ''Ungainly'', literally unhandsome, not pleasing to the eye, is applied generally to awkwardness of appearance. ''Uncouth'', literally unknown, uncommon, and so, by a bit of human conceit, uninstructed, untrained, unrefined, sometimes even rude, barbarous: as, ''uncouth'' phrases, manners. ''Bungling'', awkward in doing, handling awkwardly, spoiling by awkwardness, in either literal or figurative use: as, he made ''bungling'' work of it.}}

<poem>With ridiculous and ''awkward'' action . . .
He pageants us.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., i. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|Besides Hepzibah’s disadvantages of person, there was an uncouthness pervading all her deeds; a ''clumsy'' something, that could but ill adapt itself for use, and not at all for ornament.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, ix.}}}}

{{smaller block|Who would have predicted that the prince of Grecian eloquence should have been found in a stammering orphan, of feeble lungs and ''ungainly'' carriage, deprived of education by avaricious guardians?
{{right|''Everett'', Orations, II. 213.}}}}

{{smaller block|Many ''uncouth'' phrases and forgotten words seemed to her no less available than common forms.
{{right|''Stedman'', Vict. Poets, p. 126.}}}}

{{smaller block|He must be a ''bungling'' gamester who cannot win.
{{right|''Macaulay''.}}}}

'''awkwardly''' (âk′wärd-li), ''adv.'' In an awkward manner. {{smaller|(''a'') Clumsily; without dexterity or grace in action; in a rude or bungling manner; inelegantly. (''b'') Embarrassingly; inconveniently: as, ''awkwardly'' fixed or situated.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
